lessons.title: Fake Bank Fraud Alert
lessons.body: The scammer wants your debit card verification number (the 3-digit code on back) and personal details to make fake purchases or steal your money.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hello, this is Sarah from First National Bank security team. We detected a suspicious charge of $2,450 on your debit card at an electronics store in Texas just 20 minutes ago. Did you make this purchase?" "To protect your account, I need to verify your identity right now. Can you tell me the numbers on the back of your debit card and your full address? If we don't act fast, someone could drain your entire account."
lessons.the_trick: The Scammer wants your card verification number (the 3-digit code on back) and personal details to make fake purchases or steal your money. They create urgency by claiming a recent "suspicious charge" to pressure you into sharing sensitive info immediately.
lessons.consequences: If they get your card details, they can buy thousands of dollars in goods online or withdraw cash from ATMs. Your bank account could be emptied in hours, and recovering the money might take months or never happen.
danger_signs: Real banks never ask for full card numbers over the phone.
They know details about a "recent charge" but pressure you to verify first.
Caller ID shows unfamiliar or blocked number.
They demand immediate action without giving you time to think.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up immediately. Call your bank using the number on the back of your card or their official website (never use the number the caller gives you). Check your account online yourself to see if there's any real problem.

lessons.title: Medicare Reactivation Scam
lessons.body: The scammer pretends your Medicare benefits are about to expire to get your Medicare ID and Social Security number.
lessons.scammer_says: "Good morning, this is Mark from Medicare Services. Our records show your Medicare coverage expires next week because your card number didn't match our database. To reactivate it before you lose doctor visits and prescriptions, press 1 now and give us your Medicare number and Social Security number." "Don't worry, this takes just 2 minutes. Without this, you'll pay full price for all medical care."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer pretends your Medicare benefits are about to expire to get your Medicare ID and Social Security number. They use an automated recording or live caller to create panic about losing healthcare coverage.  It is easy for them to fake a Caller ID that says Medicare, so you can't rely on that to know if the call is real.
lessons.consequences: With your Medicare and Social Security numbers, they can file fake medical claims, steal your identity for loans, or sell your info on the dark web. This could lead to ruined credit and years of identity theft problems.
danger_signs: Medicare never calls asking for your ID numbers.
They threaten to cancel benefits unless you act immediately.
Automated message asks you to "press 1" or provide personal info.
They call you without you calling them first
lessons.safe_action: Hang up or ignore the call. Contact Medicare directly at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) using a known good number to verify your coverage status. Your Medicare card never expires.

lessons.title: Technical Support Pop-up Scam
lessons.body: They trick you into a fake pop-up warning on your computer, then call pretending to be tech support.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hello, I'm David from SecureTech Support. Your computer just sent us a virus alert — it's infected with dangerous malware and freezing up. Don't turn it off! Let me connect remotely to fix it." "I see 1,247 viruses already. Give me permission to access your screen, and it'll cost just $199 to clean everything. Type this web address now: support-fix247.com."
lessons.the_trick: They trick you into a fake pop-up warning on your computer, then call pretending to be tech support. The goal is remote access to install more malware, steal files, or charge your card for fake "repairs."
lessons.consequences: Remote access lets them steal passwords, bank info, photos, and personal documents. They can lock your files for ransom or use your computer for illegal activities, making you responsible.
danger_signs: Pop-up claims "virus alert" and gives a phone number to call.
They ask for remote screen access or payment for "fixes."
Real companies like Microsoft never cold-call about viruses.
They mention specific scary numbers like "1,247 viruses."
lessons.safe_action: Close the pop-up without calling. Restart your computer in Safe Mode if worried. Run a free scan with antivirus software you trust, like Windows Defender. Never allow remote access to unknown callers.

lessons.title: Grandparent Emergency Scam
lessons.body: The scammer pretends to be your grandchild in trouble (arrested, accident, etc.) and asks for emergency money via wire transfer or gift cards.
lessons.scammer_says: "Grandma? It's me, Tommy. Don't tell Mom, but I got arrested in Mexico during a school trip. The police are holding me for $4,200 bail or they deport me tomorrow." "A lawyer named Robert will call you from 555-0123 to arrange wire transfer to my account. Please help, I'm scared."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer pretends to be your grandchild in trouble (arrested, accident, etc.) and asks for emergency money via wire transfer or gift cards. A second caller posing as "lawyer" or "police" adds pressure.
lessons.consequences: Wire transfers and gift cards can't be reversed. You lose thousands with no way to recover, and real grandchildren in trouble wouldn't ask for secrecy or untraceable payments.
danger_signs: Grandchild asks you to keep it secret from parents.
They sound wrong (young voice, accent, wrong name details).
Payment requested via wire transfer, gift cards, or cryptocurrency.
"Lawyer" or "police" refuse to give verifiable contact info.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up and call your real grandchild directly using a known phone number. Never send money without verifying in person or through trusted channels.

lessons.title: Utility Bill Disconnection Threat
lessons.body: The scammer claims you have an unpaid utility bill and threatens immediate shutoff.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is the electric company collections department. Your account #4783921 is overdue by $678. We will disconnect your power in 30 minutes unless you pay now with a prepaid debit card." "Go to the store and buy a $678 Green Dot card. Read me the numbers over the phone to avoid blackout."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer claims you have an unpaid utility bill and threatens immediate shutoff. They demand instant payment via untraceable methods like prepaid cards or cryptocurrency to steal the money directly.
lessons.consequences: Once you give prepaid card numbers, the money vanishes instantly. No power gets disconnected because it was never your real utility company, and you can't get refunds from these payment methods.
danger_signs: Real utilities send written bills and give 7-30 days notice.
Demand for immediate payment in prepaid cards or other unusual payment method.
Refusal to send bill statement or accept check/credit card.
Unfamiliar phone number, not your utility's official line. (although sometimes they fake the name on Caller ID)
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Call your utility company using the number on your bill or website. Check your account balance online or in person. Real companies never demand instant prepaid card payments over the phone.

lessons.title: Delivery Package Scam
lessons.body: Fake text or email about a "missed delivery" tricks you into clicking links or calling.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hi, this is Acme package delivery service. We attempted delivery of your item #TX847392 today but couldn't reach you. There's a $3.95 redelivery fee or the package returns to sender tomorrow." "Click this link or call 1-877-555-0198 to pay with your credit card. We need your address for confirmation."
lessons.the_trick: You receive a text or email about a "missed delivery" that tricks you into clicking links or calling their scam phone numbers. They collect credit card numbers and addresses under the pretense of small "redelivery fees."
lessons.consequences: They steal your credit card information and use it themselves, or they collect personally identifiable information under the guise of verification which they later use to open lines of credit in your name.  If you click a link in a text or email, it may install malware that spies on you and steals banking information.
danger_signs: Unsolicited message about a package you didn't order.
Link to pay a tiny fee ($1-5) or the package will not be delivered.
No legitimate tracking number is provided upfront.
Urgent deadline (today/tomorrow) for payment.
lessons.safe_action: Delete the message. Check your real delivery accounts (UPS, FedEx, USPS) using official apps or websites. Real companies leave notices at door or send from known email/text domains.

lessons.title: Fake Charity Disaster Appeal
lessons.body: Scammers call after real disasters pretending to be charity.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hello, I'm calling from Heartland Relief Fund for hurricane victims. We've set up emergency shelters but need $50 donations now. Can you please help with donation right now? A contribution from your credit card number is tax-deductible!" "Every dollar helps families right now. We'll mail receipt tomorrow."
lessons.the_trick: Scammers call after real disasters pretending to be charity. They collect credit card donations directly over phone, but the fake organization keeps all money for themselves.
lessons.consequences: Your card info gets used for repeated unauthorized charges. No aid reaches the victims, no tax receipt arrives, and legitimate charities lose trust from the scam confusion.
danger_signs: Soliciting credit card donations cold-call style.
Vague charity name you've never heard of.
Pressure for immediate donation during disaster news.
No website or charity registration number provided.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Donate directly through known charities like Red Cross at redcross.org or local churches. Verify organizations at charitynavigator.org or guidestar.org before giving.

lessons.title: Fake Refund Overpayment
lessons.body: Claims you’re owed a refund from recent purchase to gain remote computer access.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is Amazon refund department. We overcharged you $347.62 on your recent blender purchase. To receive the refund, download this software and let us connect to your computer for 2 minutes." "Type teamviewer.com now and share the ID screen with me."
lessons.the_trick: Claims you’re owed a refund from recent purchase to gain remote computer access. While "processing the refund," they install malware and steal banking passwords or personal data.
lessons.consequences: The scammers convince you to download the software, but it isn't really to get a refund.  Instead, it installs malware which can be used to steal your banking and email passwords and enabling account takeovers across banks and email.
danger_signs: Unsolicited refund offer you didn't request.
Requires computer access or software download.
Real companies email refunds, not call for access.
They know purchase details to sound legitimate.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check your real account (Amazon, store website) for legitimate refund notices. Companies deposit refunds automatically or mail checks — they NEVER need remote access.

lessons.title: Mystery Shopper Job Scam
lessons.body: Fake job offer asks you to buy gift cards, then send card numbers/photos.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations! You have been approved for our mystery shopper position. Here's your first assignment: buy $950 in gift cards at the grocery store, take photos of receipts, then text us the card numbers for reimbursement." "You'll be reimbursed for the purchase PLUS earn $250 commission! Scratch off the back and read all numbers now."
lessons.the_trick: They claim that they will reimburse you for the purchases, and get you to give them gift card numbers. They use the cards immediately while promising reimbursement that never arrives.
lessons.consequences: You lose hundreds spent on gift cards. Scammers drain cards instantly for cash or online purchases. Legitimate employers never ask employees to buy gift cards for payment.
danger_signs: A job that pays you to buy and send gift card numbers.
No formal application or interview process.
Email/text from free services like Gmail.
"Too good to be true" high pay for simple tasks.
lessons.safe_action: Delete the offer or hangup. Real mystery shopper jobs come from established companies with websites, paychecks, and never require you to buy gift cards. Search company name + "scam" online first.

lessons.title: Romance Relationship Scam
lessons.body: Builds fake online romance over weeks/months, then invents emergencies (sick relative, travel trouble) needing urgent wire transfers.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hi Linda, it's David from the dating site. I've enjoyed getting to know you over the past several weeks. I was planning to come visit, but my sister was in an accident and I gave her $1,800 for her surgery. Now I can't buy the $400 plane ticket to come see you." "I'll get the money back from her when she recovers, and I'll pay you back then, but to get the ticket at this price, can you wire the cost of the ticket to my account please? I can't wait to see you! ❤️"
lessons.the_trick: The scammer builds fake online romance over weeks/months, then invents emergencies (sick relative, travel trouble) needing urgent wire transfers. The relationship provides emotional leverage for money requests.
lessons.consequences: The scammer gets any money or gifts you send, but the relationship is fake. Victims lose savings and suffer emotional betrayal.
danger_signs: Person avoids video calls or in-person meetings.
Sudden money requests after building the "relationship."
Always has emergencies needing wire transfers/gift cards.
Profile photos look professional, or created by AI.
lessons.safe_action: Never send money to online contacts. Verify their identity through video call or mutual friends. Report relationshp scams to FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (ic3.gov) and dating site. Real relationships develop without money requests.

lessons.title: IRS Tax Refund Scam
lessons.body: The scammer pretends the IRS owes you money to collect bank account details for direct deposit.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is the Internal Revenue Service. You have an unclaimed refund of $1,872 waiting. Due to a filing error, we need your bank routing number and account number to direct deposit it today." "Press 1 to claim before funds return to Treasury, or call 1-888-555-0284."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer pretends the IRS owes you money to collect bank account details for direct deposit. The real IRS never calls unexpectedly about refunds or demands immediate bank info over phone.
lessons.consequences: Bank details let them drain accounts or create fake checks. IRS identity theft leads to tax problems, frozen refunds, and years repairing credit/government records.
danger_signs: IRS never calls demanding immediate bank info.
They mention an "unclaimed refund" you were not expecting
The call is from an automated message or unknown 800-number.
They threaten that the funds will expire unless you act now.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. IRS sends refund checks by mail or direct deposits already on file. Check your status at irs.gov using your own computer; never call numbers from unsolicited messages.

lessons.title: Home Repair Contractor Scam
lessons.body: A repairman knocks on your door, claiming urgent damage that only they spotted.
lessons.scammer_says: "Ma'am, this is Mike's Roofing from down the street. I noticed you have some damaged shingles while driving by. Storm damage like this costs $8,000 to fix later, but I can do it today for $2,800 cash." "Pay half now, I'll start immediately before rain worsens it."
lessons.the_trick: A repairman knocks on your door, claiming urgent damage that only they spotted. They take a large cash deposit then disappear or do shoddy work. Real roof issues don't require instant payment.
lessons.consequences: Cash is gone and unrecoverable.  If they do work, it may be poor quality resulting in further damage.
danger_signs: Unsolicited door knock claiming urgent home repair.
Cash payment demanded upfront.
No written estimate or business license shown.
Pressure to decide immediately.
lessons.safe_action: Say no thanks. Get 3 written estimates from licensed contractors with reviews. Never pay more than 10% deposit. Check business license at state contractor board website.

lessons.title: Lottery Prize Scam
lessons.body: The scammer claims you won lottery/sweepstakes you don't remember entering.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations! You won $250,000 in the National Sweepstakes drawing. Your entry #M7392847 was selected! To claim this grand prize, send $498 processing fee and taxes via MoneyGram to our agent in Florida." "Winners must pay fees first. Call 1-800-555-0317."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer claims you won a lottery or sweepstakes you do not remember entering. They demand "fees" (taxes, processing) via wire transfer before payout. Real winnings never require upfront payment.
lessons.consequences: Once they have your payment information, they can use it to steal your money.  No prize exists. Wired money is gone forever. Your credit could be ruined if they get enough personal info for identity theft.
danger_signs: You never entered contest but "won."
Upfront fees are required to claim prize.
You must make payment by wire transfer/MoneyGram.
The prize amounts are too good to be true.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up — real prizes never ask for money first. Verify at official lottery website. Report to FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Legitimate winnings contact you formally.

lessons.title: Government Grant Scam
lessons.body: The scammer claims you have been awarded a government grant for home repair/education.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations! You qualify for a $5,000 government home improvement grant. No repayment is needed. Send the $250 processing fee to Federal Grant Processing Center via a prepaid debit card." "There are limited spots — pay today to lock in funds!"
lessons.the_trick: The small "application fee" via prepaid cards is taken by the scammer.  There is no real grant.  Real grants never charge applicants to receive the funds.
lessons.consequences: Prepaid card money is gone instantly. No grant exists. Any information you give could be used for identity theft.
danger_signs: Government "free money" requires upfront fees.
Email/text from generic domains (like gmail.com).
Payment is requested via prepaid cards or wire transfer.
Unsolicited grant offers you never applied for.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Real grants through grants.gov require applications, never fees. Contact legitimate agencies directly. Report to ftc.gov/complaint.

lessons.title: Pharmacy Discount Scam
lessons.body: Unsolicited offer of prescription discounts asks for Medicare/health info.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is National Pharmacy Services. We can cut your prescriptions by 85% with our discount card. Just give us your Medicare number and doctor's name to activate lifetime savings." "No cost to join — text back YES to enroll!"
lessons.the_trick: An unsolicited offer of prescription discounts asks for your Medicare/health info. Fake "discount cards" steal insurance details to make fraudulent claims and commit identity theft.
lessons.consequences: Medicare fraud can be billed to your number. They can create fraudulent identities which can impact your actual account, causing confusion and expenses.
danger_signs: Unsolicited prescription discount offers.
They ask for Medicare/pharmacy benefit numbers.
Any text message from short codes or unknown numbers.
A "discount" card that sounds too good to verify.
lessons.safe_action: Delete the text or email message (or hang up). Use legitimate discount cards from GoodRx.com or your pharmacy chain. Never share your Medicare number with discount services. Report to Medicare at 1-800-MEDICARE.

lessons.title: Apartment Rental Scam
lessons.body: You respond to fake listings with pretty photos and a deal that's too good to be true.
lessons.scammer_says: "Reserve this perfect 2-bedroom apartment, only $1,200/month available immediately! Great photos online. Send a $1,200 deposit via Zelle to hold it before it's gone. Here's my number: 555-0199." "We're moving out of state, and need a renter fast!"
lessons.the_trick: They post fake apartment listings with stolen photos. They take deposits via app transfers then disappear. The apartment doesn't exist or the real owner knows nothing about rental.
lessons.consequences: Money sent as a 'deposit' is lost and not recoverable.
danger_signs: No in-person viewing allowed.
Landlord demands full deposit via app before seeing unit.
"Moving fast, must pay now" pressure.
Listing photos look professionally staged.
lessons.safe_action: Never send money without seeing the apartment in person. Meet the landlord/owner at the property. Use a written lease. Verify the listing at apartmentratings.com. Only pay with cashier's check and only after a tour.

lessons.title: Car Warranty Scam
lessons.body: You receive a call claiming that your car warranty is ending.  The scammer uses vague vehicle details to sound legitimate.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is Auto Protection Services. Your car warranty expires tomorrow. To avoid costly repairs in the event of an issue with your car, you can extend your coverage. $399 locks in any defect repairs for 5 years. Press 1 to speak Spanish or stay on line." " Your VIN ending 8472 is confirmed as approved for this discount. Provide your credit card details for payment and we can guarantee this rate."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer lies about being with your warranty company, and uses vague details about your vehicle to sound convincing.  They will take your credit card information and use it for fraudulent charges
lessons.consequences: Once they have your credit card details they can use it to make fraudulent purchases, possibly impacting your balance and credit score.
danger_signs: Any call about car warranty expiration.
Pressure for an immediate payment decision.
No specific warranty details provided.
"Last chance" expiration threats.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check the real warranty through your car dealership service department or manufacturer's website, or with your own warranty company. Use your existing warranty paperwork to find a verified, trusted phone number.  Remember, no harm will come by hanging up.

lessons.title: Social Security Scam
lessons.body: A caller claiming to be with the Social Security Administration threatens to suspend benefits unless you "verify" SSN over phone.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is the Social Security Administration fraud department. Suspicious activity using your SSN has been detected, and requires immediate suspension. Verify your identity by providing your full Social Security number and birthdate." "Failure to comply may trigger law enforcement action."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer threatens to suspend your Social Security benefits unless you "verify" your SSN over phone. The real Social Security Administration never calls demanding immediate personal information verification.
lessons.consequences: Providing details like SSN and birthdate enables identity theft, fake benefit claims, and potentially loans taken out in your name.
danger_signs: Social Security Administration demands SSN over phone.
Threats of arrest or benefit suspension.
Caller ID spoofing government numbers.
Urgent verification pressure.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Create mySocialSecurity account at ssa.gov to check your actual status. Contact the SSA at its known, trusted number (1-800-772-1213). Report scams to oig.ssa.gov.

lessons.title: Investment Scam
lessons.body: A cold call pitches "guaranteed high returns" investments.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hi Margaret, I'm Tom from Prosperity Investments. Our green energy fund returns 28% annually — double your neighbor's gains! Invest $10,000 minimum via wire transfer today." "You qualify as a new investor, but shares are limited so this opportunity is closing fast."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer makes claims of "guaranteed high return" investments. They steal payment information and use it for fraudulent purchases.
lessons.consequences: Complete loss of your investment principal. Wire transfers are unrecoverable. The fake company vanishes. Retirement savings can be wiped out chasing unrealistic returns.
danger_signs: "Guaranteed" high investment returns.
Cold call from unknown firm.
Wire transfer or crypto payment required.
Pressure to invest immediately.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Verify firm at sec.gov/EDGAR or finra.org/brokercheck. Work only with registered advisors. Investments promising guaranteed high returns = scams.

lessons.title: Jury Duty Arrest Scam
lessons.body: The scammer claims you missed jury duty and there is a warrant requiring immediate "bail" payment via prepaid cards.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is the County Sheriff's Office. You missed your jury duty summons and a warrant has been issued for your arrest. Post $1,000 bail via prepaid cards or appear in 60 minutes at the central station downtown." "This is officer Simmons, badge #8472. Do not hang up or the warrant activates."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer claims you missed jury duty and there is a warrant requiring immediate "bail" payment via prepaid cards. Real police make arrests in person, and never demand payment over phone.
lessons.consequences: Any payments made are lost and not recoverable.
danger_signs: Police demand prepaid cards or wire transfer.
Threat of immediate arrest over phone.
"Badge number" provided to sound official.
Refuse to verify through official channels.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Police arrest in person with a uniformed officer and warrant. Call your local courthouse using 411 directory assistance number to verify status. Report to ftc.gov.

lessons.title: Magazine Prize Scam
lessons.body: Impersonates famous sweepstakes company claiming big win.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations! You won $5,000 from Publisher's Clearing House sweepstakes! Magazine subscriptions entered you automatically. Send $495 shipping/handling via MoneyGram to claim your prize before 5PM today." "Are you available tomorrow for the big check and flowers to be delivered?"
lessons.the_trick: The scammer impersonates a famous sweepstakes company claiming a big win.  States you must pay a "shipping fees" via wire transfer. Real prizes never require payment to receive winnings.
lessons.consequences: Fees are stolen, and any payment information you give will be used fraudulently.
danger_signs: Prize requires payment first.
"Shipping/handling" fees for large winnings.
MoneyGram/wire transfer demanded.
"Winning" a contest you never entered.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Real sweepstakes winners are notified by mail.  Never pay to collect a prize.

lessons.title: Free Trial Scam
lessons.body: The scammer uses the promise of a free trial to collect, and later bill, recurring payments.
lessons.scammer_says: "Congratulations!  You have been approved for a free 30-day trial of HealthMax Vitamins! Confirm your shipping address and credit card for $4.95 processing. Cancel anytime after first shipment." "After your free trial, monthly shipments will be $89.95 each, but you can cancel any time."
lessons.the_trick: A small "shipping fee" enrolls you in expensive monthly subscription which is hard to cancel, and charges your card repeatedly.  Trying to cancel is difficult with phone number disconnects, long hold times, etc.
lessons.consequences: The recurring billing can charge hundreds of dollars for an unwanted product. Cancellation battles fail.
danger_signs: "Free trial" asks for credit card upfront.
Small fee seems like a good deal for a free trial.
Hard-to-find cancellation instructions.
Multiple shipments promised automatically.
lessons.safe_action: Never give your card for "free trials." Use virtual credit cards or prepaid debit (with very limited funds on the card) for testing, and only on products that you initiate (not in response to a call). Dispute scam charges with your bank.

lessons.title: Vaccine Certificate Scam
lessons.body: Fake government health verification demands Medicare info and fees.
lessons.scammer_says: "Health Department records show you need COVID vaccine verification in order to receive your Medicare coverage. Pay $39.95 processing fee in order to receive the official digital certificate." "Email your Medicare number and card details to verify eligibility."
lessons.the_trick: Fake government health verification tries to either collect payment information, or Medicare information.  Either they make fraudulent charges using your credit card, or submit fraudulent Medicare claims using your information.
lessons.consequences: Costs of stolen payments, and challenges trying to resolve fraudulent Medicare claims made in your name.
danger_signs: Email or call demands Medicare info for vaccine certificates.
Payment required for official government health documents.
Unofficial websites selling vaccine proof.
Urgent threats to Medicare payments.
lessons.safe_action: Delete text or email message or hang up. Real vaccine records come from your healthcare provider only. Your Medicare status is not in jeopardy, but you can confirm at 1-800-MEDICARE.

lessons.title: Storage Unit Scam
lessons.body: Fake "neighbor" sells nonexistent storage auction contents cheap.
lessons.scammer_says: "Hi neighbor, it's Jim from across the street. My storage unit #247 at Mini-Store is auctioning tomorrow for unpaid rent. The contents are worth $8,000 but you can have them for $500 cash today.  It's more than I'd get at auction, and I can clear the bill." "There is furniture, tools, and some antiques — meet me at the unit at 3:30PM."
lessons.the_trick: Fake "neighbor" tricks you into bringing cash, meeting at a storage unit. Then the scammer takes your cash and drives away.
lessons.consequences: Your cash is lost instantly. No storage unit exists. Scammer offered a deal too sweet to pass up to entice you to bring cash to a private location.
danger_signs: "Neighbor" you don't recognize selling storage contents.
Cash deal for valuable auction items.
No public auction listing or inspection.
Same-day "must buy now" pressure.
lessons.safe_action: Call storage facility directly to verify the existence of an auction. Attend public auctions only. Never buy sight-unseen valuables for cash from strangers.  Never meet a stranger when they know you'll be bringing cash.

lessons.title: Toll Violation Scam
lessons.body: Fake toll violations demand prepaid card payment.
lessons.scammer_says: This is the Toll Authority Collections — Your vehicle with license #JHG-8472 has 6 unpaid tolls totaling $287 from the State Turnpike. Pay the balance now or your vehicle's registration will be suspended. Provide payment details to our agent or face up to  $500 fine and your vehicle could be towed.
lessons.the_trick: Fake toll violations demand prepaid card payment. Real toll agencies mail invoices, and accept checks/credit cards.
lessons.consequences: Your payment information will be used to rack up fake charges.
danger_signs: Toll payment demanded over the phone.
Phone threats of registration suspension or towing.
Unfamiliar agency name/number.
No mailed invoice provided.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check your toll balance at your state's official toll website. Real agencies mail bills first.

lessons.title: School Trip Emergency
lessons.body: Two-call scam: grandchild claims group travel emergency, fake teacher confirms.
lessons.scammer_says: "Grandma, it's Sarah from the school trip to Washington DC. Our bus broke down in Georgia, and we need $250 cash per student or the whole group will be stranded overnight. Talk to my teacher to get the Western Union information so we can get a bus now."
lessons.the_trick: Two-call scam: fake grandchild claims there is a group travel emergency, a fake teacher confirms. Real school trips have emergency funds and insurance.
lessons.consequences: Western Union money that you wire is gone instantly and not recoverable. In reality, no school trip problems exist and the grandchild is likely safe at home.
danger_signs: Grandchild + teacher both call about group emergency.
School demands Western Union for trip issues.
Sudden "everyone stranded" pressure.
Contacting a grandparent instead of guardian or school authorities.
lessons.safe_action: Call the grandchild's home phone and school directly. Real emergencies go through the child's designated guardian first. Schools handle trip insurance.

lessons.title: Church Directory Scam
lessons.body: Fake church directory sales to members.
lessons.scammer_says: "Grace Community Church is publishing a directory. Your photo and family listing is $125 for a full page, $89 for a half page. Provide credit card info to reserve the professional photographer for a session tomorrow. All the other members are participating — don't miss out!"
lessons.the_trick: Fake church directory sales to members. No directory is produced. The church knows nothing about the solicitation.
lessons.consequences: You lose the payment and possibly the card will be used for recurring charges.
danger_signs: Church directory sales by phone.
No church announcement or bulletin notice.
Payment before seeing proofs.
Multiple family photo packages offered.
lessons.safe_action: Call the church office directly to verify. Real directories are announced in services, and payment is made after proofs are seen.

lessons.title: Fence Contractor Scam
lessons.body: The scammer knocks on the door, claiming you have a code violation with your fence.
lessons.scammer_says: "Ace Fence Company is canvassing neighborhood. Your fence is leaning dangerously — it's a code violation risk.  I can do it for only $1500 for a full replacement today, or for $750 just for repairs.  We'll need half in cash to get started.  Be aware that the county inspector is coming to this neighborhood next week — avoid the fine by repairing it now!"
lessons.the_trick: A door-to-door scammer claims you have fence code violations. Asks for a cash deposit then either does poor work or disappears. Threatens that you will get a fine if you don't repair the fence.  But real violations get written county notices.
lessons.consequences: Cash is lost and not recoverable.
danger_signs: Door-to-door fence "code violation" warnings.
Asking for cash deposit up front.
No written county violation notice.
Inspector "next week" pressure.
lessons.safe_action: Request written violation from the county first. Get 3 licensed contractor bids. Never pay cash deposits.

lessons.title: Identity Protection Scam
lessons.body: Fake identity theft alerts demand full personal info access.
lessons.scammer_says: "IdentityGuard alert — your Social Security number appears on 7 dark web sites.  Protect yourself with a $29.95/month monitoring service that will remove your information from the dark web. Provide your SSN and payment information to enroll. The first month is free if you start now!"
lessons.the_trick: Fake identity theft alerts demand full personal info access. Real monitoring services let you sign up without sharing your SSN over the phone.
lessons.consequences: Theft of your identity, along with payment information.
danger_signs: Identity service demands SSN/passwords.
"Dark web" alerts requiring full access.
Urgent enrollment pressure.
$29.95 sounds reasonably low.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Check your credit at annualcreditreport.com (free). Real services monitor externally, and never access accounts.  Visit the FTC identitytheft.gov official site for real help.

lessons.title: Tech Support Gift Card Scam
lessons.body: Fake tech support demands gift card purchases for "virus removal fees." They drain cards instantly while you watch.
lessons.scammer_says: "Microsoft technical support here. Your computer has 847 viruses detected. Don't panic — we can clear your computer.  Normally the fix is $249, but we partner with Google for a massive discount - you buy a $100 Google Play gift card from your local pharmacy or grocery store immediately. That gift card will qualify you for the discount. Scratch off the back, and read the 15-digit numbers to me now, and you can make your computer safe for the discounted price."
lessons.the_trick: Fake tech support demands gift card purchases for "virus removal fees." They drain cards instantly while you watch.
lessons.consequences: $100 gone in seconds. Gift cards are untraceable. The computer may not have had viruses, but if they did, the scammers won't fix them.
danger_signs: Tech support encourages gift card payments.
"847 viruses detected" - specific scary numbers.
Microsoft never cold-calls about viruses.
Immediate store purchase pressure.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Run Windows Defender scan (free). Real tech support never requests gift cards. Report the call to ftc.gov.

lessons.title: Online Car Sale Scam
lessons.body: Fake car listing requires deposit to steal your money.
lessons.scammer_says: You see an online ad that looks really good: 2019 Toyota Camry 42K miles $12,500 FIRM — moving overseas, must sell fast! Email shipping deposit $1,200 via PayPal Friends & Family to hold car. Broker arranges delivery to your driveway!"
lessons.the_trick: There is no car, the listing is fake.  Once you send the 'deposit', you cannot recover that money, and there is no tracing the seller, who disappears with your money.
lessons.consequences: Scammer takes your deposit, and possibly more depending on how much payment information you provided.
danger_signs: Too-good deal on a popular car.
Seller is "moving overseas" and won't meet in person to preview the car.
PayPal Friends & Family requested.
Shipping broker handles delivery.
lessons.safe_action: Always test drive in person. Pay using dealer/bank check only. Verify the car's VIN at carfax.com. Never wire money for unseen vehicles.

lessons.title: Funeral Prepayment Scam
lessons.body: Fake funeral preplanning steals life savings.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is Eternal Rest Planning Services.  Avoid the stress and confusion of your loved ones in the event of your demise.  Prepare by locking in funeral costs at today's rates and protect against inflation!  Set aside $3.700 into a prepaid trust fund which guarantees a mahogany casket, a plot in the cemetery of your choice, and costs of a graveside service regardless of inflation. Let's setup this trust for you today."
lessons.the_trick: Fake funeral preplanning steals life savings. No funeral services provided when needed. Real preplanning through licensed funeral homes only.
lessons.consequences: In spite of good intentions to protect your family, your money is put into a trust where you lose control of it, and have no recourse.
danger_signs: Unsolicited funeral prepayment offers.
Wire transfer to "funeral trust."
No licensed funeral home connection.
High-pressure "lock in today's rates."
lessons.safe_action: Plan directly with local licensed funeral homes. Use payable-on-death life insurance. Verify at funerals.org. Never prepay sight-unseen.

lessons.title: Solar Panel Rebate Scam
lessons.body: Fake government solar rebates demand processing fees.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is the Federal Solar Energy Program.  The Department of Energy is offering an $8,500 rebate on solar panels, but it expires next month! Qualify now with a $995 processing deposit to the Energy Department trust. Panels will be installed for free after approval.  The government pays the installation — you keep rebate!"
lessons.the_trick: Fake government solar rebates demand processing fees. No panels installed, no rebate issued.
lessons.consequences: $995 lost to nonexistent program. Real solar incentives are through tax credits only.
danger_signs: Government "rebates" require upfront fees.
Solar panels promised "free after approval."
Energy Department trust fund payments.
Phone calls, not mailed applications.
lessons.safe_action: Government rebate programs change, so search official government sites, not depending on a stranger calling to provide the information. The government never demands deposits for rebates.

lessons.title: Grandchild Phone Scam
lessons.body: Two-scammer relay: "grandchild" claims lost phone, can't call parents.
lessons.scammer_says: "Grandma it's Alex — I lost my phone at the fair, I'm calling from the Apple store, which is why you don't recognize the number. I need a $300 iPhone deposit at Apple Store or I'm stranded till Dad returns Tuesday. Can you put it on your card, and I'll repay cash Friday?  Here's the Apple store salesperson to help with the details...❤️"
lessons.the_trick: Two-scammer relay: "grandchild" claims they lost their phone, and can't call parents. The real grandchild has phone, and is safe at home.
lessons.consequences: You lose the payment to the fake Apple store, and possibly future fraudulent purchases made with your credit card information.
danger_signs: Grandchild calling from "borrowed phone."
Can't call parents, only grandparents.
Sudden expensive phone replacement.
Repayment promised but urgent now.
lessons.safe_action: Tell them you will call back.  Hang up, and call your grandchild's number. Then verify with their parents or guardian.

lessons.title: Driveway Sealing Scam
lessons.body: Door-to-door driveway "sealing" with watered-down asphalt.
lessons.scammer_says: "We mixed more sealant than your neighbor needed, and it's just going to go to waste.  We've got the truck right here, and we can seal coat your driveway right now.  We can give you a huge discount if you pay cash."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer goes door-to-door with watered-down asphalt.  It peels off in weeks (if they even coat anything at all).
lessons.consequences: You lose the cash with no way to recover it.
danger_signs: Door-to-door driveway sealing offers.
Claims they have extra which will go to waste.
Cash only, immediate start pressure.
No written contract/estimate.
lessons.safe_action: If you want your driveway sealed, get three written bids from licensed pavers. Avoid paying cash deposits.

lessons.title: Timeshare Cancellation Scam
lessons.body: Fake timeshare cancellation services take escrow fees but never resolve ownership.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is the Timeshare Relief Team — we legally dissolve your maintenance fee burden!  Once we receive the $2,500 escrow deposit, we guarantee your timeshare cancellation within 90 days or  you receive a full refund. We have a deed transfer specialist standing by."
lessons.the_trick: Fake timeshare cancellation services take escrow fees but never resolve ownership. Timeshare remains, fees continue.
lessons.consequences: You lose the 'deposit', and you still have the obligation to the time share dues.
danger_signs: Timeshare "cancellation guarantees."
Upfront escrow thousands required.
No attorney licensing shown.
90-day miracle promises.
lessons.safe_action: Contact your timeshare developer directly, or seek out a Licensed real estate attorney only.  Do not respond to calls initiated by someone else that asks for financial information.

lessons.title: IRS Audit Scam
lessons.body: Fake IRS audit demands immediate bank access.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is the IRS Audit Compliance Division — your last tax return #847392 was flagged for an underpayment amount of $3,247. You need to pay the penalty via our secure portal or face liens and/or levies. Go to payirsbill.net and use case #45872 to resolve this issue, or face increased legal consequences."
lessons.the_trick: Fake IRS audit demands immediate bank access. Real IRS sends certified mail first, never phone demands.
lessons.consequences: Depending on what information they collect, the scammers can drain your bank accounts to zero.  Never visit a website provided by a stranger to enter payment information.
danger_signs: IRS demands bank info over phone.
No certified mail received first.
Immediate payment portal pressure.
"Letter to follow" excuse.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. The real IRS makes contact by mail. NEVER visit a website provided by a stranger to enter payment information.

lessons.title: Verification Number Scam
lessons.summary: The scammer claims to be from your bank, and sends you a verification number to read it to them.
lessons.body: A scammer will call claiming a problem with one of your financial accounts.  They claim they need to verify you are the authorized account holder, so they will send a code to your phone.  The code is from your bank, but they need to know it to access your account.  If you tell them the code, they will be able to access your account.
lessons.scammer_says: "There is a problem with your bank account.  But first I need to verify your identity.  Please confirm your email address....  Very good, that's right.  We have sent a text code to your phone to ensure you are the authorized user of this account.  Please read the numbers so we can verify you."
lessons.the_trick: They are trying to login to your account, but need the authentication from your mobile device.  The bank automatically generates a code and sends it to your phone.  They cannot get in without it, but if you provide it, they will have full access to your accounts.
lessons.consequences: They can take all the money from your accounts, reroute notification information to another email address so you are not notified, and also use your information to take out further loans.
danger_signs: NO ONE should ever ask you to read the verification number from your mobile device.
They called you, but need you to verify yourself.
Urgency to resolve a problem fast, with dire consequences if you hang up.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up and call your bank using a verified, trusted number.  If there is a problem, they will connect you to the right person, and no harm will be done by hanging up on the initial call.  Banks do not initiate calls that then require you to verify yourself.

lessons.title: Verification Screen Scam
lessons.summary: A fake verification screen asks you for a series of keystrokes that installs malware without your knowledge.
lessons.body: A fake verification screen asks you for a series of keystrokes that installs malware without your knowledge.
lessons.scammer_says: A "verification window" pops up on your computer.  It asks you to do a series of keystrokes like 'WIN + R, then CTRL + V, then Enter' to verify.
lessons.the_trick: The keystrokes requested open a command prompt on your computer, then pastes a bad command in.  They have put a bad command on your clipboard (usually by having you click something on the screen before the popup), then WIN + R opens the command prompt, CTRL + V pastes what they put on the clipboard, and Enter runs it.
lessons.consequences: Once the command is run, this could install malware that they can use to steal files, banking information, email account information, or lock your computer for ransom.
danger_signs: Pop-up windows for Verification
Asking for specific commands like WIN + R and CTRL + V
Any verification that opens another window
lessons.safe_action: Never use that keystroke combination (WIN or Windows Key + R, CTRL or Control + V).

lessons.title: AI Voice Clone Family Emergency
lessons.body: A scammer uses AI to mimic a loved one's voice and demands urgent payment.
lessons.scammer_says: "Mom? It's me. I got in a bad car accident. Please don't call Dad yet — I'm with the police and my phone is about to die. They say I need $1,500 for a tow and medical fee right now. Can you send it by Zelle to this number? Please hurry!"
lessons.the_trick: They use short, emotional audio (or a shaky phone call) to make you think you're hearing your child or grandchild. AI voice-cloning can copy tone and cadence from short clips posted online. The panic is designed to stop you from verifying.
lessons.consequences: You send money to the scammer, and it’s hard or impossible to reverse. They may keep calling for more payments and may target other family members if you share details.
danger_signs: They demand secrecy ("don’t call Dad" / "don’t tell anyone").
They insist on urgent payment by Zelle, or gift cards.
They avoid a callback to a known number or refuse video.
The story changes when you ask simple verification questions.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Call your loved one using a known number (or contact another family member). If you can’t reach them, call the relevant institution directly (hospital, school, or local police) using a verified number.

lessons.title: Zelle Overpayment Refund Scam
lessons.body: A buyer “accidentally” sends too much money and pressures you to refund the difference before the payment is reversed.
lessons.scammer_says: "Oops — I sent $1,200 instead of $120 for the item you sold me on the online marketplace. Please send back $1,080 right now by Zelle. I’m at work and can’t fix it. If you don’t refund me in 10 minutes, I’ll report you for theft."
lessons.the_trick: The “payment” is often fake (screenshots), sent from a compromised account, or later disputed. They try to get you to send real money back quickly. When the original transfer is reversed or never existed, you’re out the refund amount.
lessons.consequences: You lose the refund money you sent. If you shared bank details or clicked a link, your accounts could be compromised.
danger_signs: They show screenshots instead of you seeing money in your own app.
They pressure you to send a refund immediately.
They request the refund to a different name/number than the original sender.
They threaten you with police reports or platform bans to rush you.
lessons.safe_action: Do not send any refund via Zelle. Only refund through the original platform’s official process (or cancel and wait). If money truly arrived, contact your bank/Zelle support for guidance before sending anything back.

lessons.title: Investment “Account Locked” Impersonation
lessons.body: A scammer claims your invetment account is locked and tries to steal your login, verification codes, or remote access.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is your Investment Broker's security department. We detected a login from a new device in another state. Your account will be frozen in 15 minutes. To verify you, read me the 6-digit code we just texted you. Then download our secure support app so I can remove the hacker."
lessons.the_trick: They impersonate support and push you to share one-time passcodes or approve a login. Sometimes they ask for remote access to “fix” the account. The goal is to take over your brokerage account and move money out.
lessons.consequences: They can take over your account, change your email/phone, place trades, or attempt withdrawals. Cleaning up a brokerage takeover can be slow and stressful.
danger_signs: They ask for your one-time passcode (OTP) or authentication code.
They tell you to install remote-access or “support” software.
They pressure you with a short deadline ("15 minutes").
They give you a link/number and insist you must use it.
lessons.safe_action: Hang up. Open the official investment brokerage app/website yourself (not via a link) and check notifications. Contact support only through the app or official help pages. Never share OTP (one-time passcodes) codes with anyone.

lessons.title: Pig Butchering Crypto Investment Scam
lessons.body: A scammer builds trust over time, then convinces you to invest on a fake crypto platform that shows fake profits.
lessons.scammer_says: "I’ve been doing this strategy for months — it’s safe. Look, my account grew 18% this week. I can help you set up your online crypto wallet. Start with just $500, then add more after you see the profits. Don’t tell your bank — they don’t understand crypto."
lessons.the_trick: They groom you through online friendship or romance, then raise the topic of investing.  They are excited about the money they have made, and invite you to an “investment platform” they control. The website/app shows growing balances, but withdrawals are blocked unless you pay “taxes/fees,” which are also stolen.
lessons.consequences: You can lose everything you send. Victims often keep paying additional “fees” trying to withdraw. Recovery is uncommon.
danger_signs: An online friend pivots to investing/crypto talk.
They insist you use a specific website/app you’ve never heard of.
The platform shows big, steady gains with little risk.
Withdrawals require extra payments for “tax,” “verification,” or “unlocking.”
lessons.safe_action: Do not send money. Do not pay any “withdrawal fees.” Save evidence (screenshots, wallet addresses). Contact your bank and report the fraud to your local authorities.

lessons.title: QR Code Parking Meter Scam
lessons.body: A fake QR code sticker on a parking meter sends you to a payment site that steals your card info.
lessons.scammer_says: (the QR Code sticker on the parking meter says) 'Scan here to pay quickly.' The site looks official and asks for your card number, billing address, and phone number. After you pay, it says: "Payment failed — try again."
lessons.the_trick: Scammers place stickers over legitimate QR codes or post fake “pay here” signs. The website is designed to collect your payment details and sometimes make repeated charges.
lessons.consequences: Your card can be used for fraudulent purchases. Your personal info can also be used for identity theft or more scam targeting.
danger_signs: A QR code sticker looks newly placed or covers another label.
The payment URL looks unfamiliar or misspelled.
The site asks for extra info that feels unnecessary.
It claims “failed” and pushes you to retry immediately.
lessons.safe_action: Do not scan random QR stickers. Use the official parking app name shown on the meter/sign, or type the official website yourself. If you already entered card info, contact your bank and monitor transactions.

lessons.title: Fake Bill-Payment Search Result Scam
lessons.summary: A fake search result sends you to a lookalike bill-payment website.
lessons.body: You search online for a utility, phone, internet, medical lab, or toll bill payment page. A paid search result looks like the real company, but the website may be controlled by a scammer or an intermediary that is not the biller. You may pay unexpected fees, give away payment information, or think you paid the real company when you did not.
lessons.scammer_says: "Pay your bill quickly here — official online payment center." "You're in the right place. Just enter your account number, card number, and billing information to make your payment."
lessons.the_trick: Scammers use paid search ads, copied logos, and lookalike websites to appear connected to a real biller. The search result can look convincing even though the website is not the company's official payment channel. An intermediary may also collect the payment and add fees or misrepresent its relationship with the biller.
lessons.consequences: Your payment is stolen by the scammer, and not applied to your actual bill.  Late fees may be charged, or your payment and personal information may be exposed. You could also believe a bill was paid when the real biller never received the money.
danger_signs: The search result is a paid ad or unfamiliar website instead of the biller's known website.
The website address is slightly different from the company's official address.
The site does not clearly explain who is actually receiving the payment.
Unexpected fees or extra charges appear before you can pay.
lessons.safe_action: Do not assume the first search result is the official payment site. Type the biller's known website yourself or use its official app, then pay from your account there. Check your statement afterward to confirm the payment went to the correct company.

lessons.title: Scam Recovery or Refund Assistance
lessons.summary: A scammer promises to recover money you already lost, then asks for more money or personal information.
lessons.body: After someone loses money to a scam, the victim may be contacted by a person claiming they can recover the funds, locate a missing prize, or get a refund for undelivered merchandise. The supposed helper may pretend to be from a government agency, consumer group, or law firm. They then demand an upfront processing or administrative fee or ask for banking and identity information.
lessons.scammer_says: "We found your missing money and can recover it for you." "There is a small $450 administrative fee before we can release the funds. We also need your bank account and identification information to verify the recovery."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer targets people who have already been hurt by fraud. They use the promise of getting the lost money back to gain trust, then collect another payment or sensitive information. The recovery offer is simply another scam.
lessons.consequences: You can lose even more money after already being scammed. Banking and identity information can also be used for account theft or identity fraud.
danger_signs: Someone contacts you unexpectedly about recovering money you lost.
They demand an upfront processing, administrative, or legal fee.
They promise recovery before explaining how they verified your claim.
They ask for banking or identity information to receive the supposed recovery.
lessons.safe_action: Do not pay a recovery fee or give sensitive information to an unexpected caller. Contact the original company, payment provider, or government agency yourself using a trusted official number or website. Treat an unsolicited promise to recover lost money as another possible scam.

lessons.title: Fake FBI or IC3 Recovery Scam
lessons.summary: A scammer impersonates the FBI or IC3 and claims your stolen money has been found.
lessons.body: A scammer contacts someone who has already been victimized by fraud and pretends to be from the FBI or the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3). They may use a phone call, email, social media, messaging app, fake website, or convincing video. They claim your money has been found or that your IC3 complaint needs to be updated, then try to obtain money or sensitive information.
lessons.scammer_says: "This is an IC3 recovery specialist. We located the funds that were stolen from you." "To update your complaint and release the recovered funds, send the processing fee and confirm your bank and identity information."
lessons.the_trick: The scammer uses the authority of the FBI or IC3 to make the victim believe the recovery is official. The FBI says IC3 has no social-media presence and does not recover funds through social platforms or messaging apps. The goal is to exploit a person who has already lost money.
lessons.consequences: You can lose additional money, expose your bank or identity information, and give scammers more information about your previous fraud victimization.
danger_signs: Someone claiming to be IC3 contacts you through social media or a messaging app.
They say your stolen money has been found and requires a fee to release.
They ask for banking, identity, or authentication information.
They pressure you to update a complaint through a link or contact method they provide.
lessons.safe_action: Do not pay or provide sensitive information to the person who contacted you. Do not trust social-media or messaging accounts claiming to represent IC3. If you need to report or follow up on a cybercrime, use the official FBI or IC3 website that you locate yourself.

lessons.title: Fake Social-Media Shopping Ad
lessons.summary: A convincing social-media ad offers a popular product at an unusually low price.
lessons.body: You see an attractive ad while scrolling through social media. It may use a familiar brand name, a dramatic discount, a countdown timer, or a limited-time offer. The ad can lead to a fake store that sends counterfeit or inferior goods, sends nothing at all, or collects your payment information. An ad appearing in a social-media feed is not proof that the seller is legitimate.
lessons.scammer_says: "Today only! Name-brand products are 80% off while supplies last." "Click now before the sale ends — thousands of customers have already ordered."
lessons.the_trick: Scammers use paid social-media advertising to reach shoppers and make fake stores look trustworthy. They use desirable products, brand names, steep discounts, and urgency to get buyers to order before checking the seller.
lessons.consequences: You may receive a counterfeit or poor-quality product, receive nothing, or expose your credit card information to a fraudulent seller. The money may be difficult to recover.
danger_signs: The price is dramatically lower than normal for a desirable brand-name product.
The ad uses strong urgency such as a countdown or "today only" offer.
The seller or website has little verifiable history outside the social-media ad.
The ad makes the product or seller look legitimate without giving you a reliable way to verify the business.
lessons.safe_action: Do not treat a social-media ad as proof that a seller is legitimate. Before buying, research the seller independently and go to the brand's known website if you want that product. Use a payment method with buyer protections when possible, and avoid rushing because of a countdown or limited-time claim.

lessons.title: Social-Media Investment Training Scam
lessons.summary: A social-media promotion promises that simple trading training can quickly lead to wealth.
lessons.body: A post or advertisement promises that ordinary people can quickly learn trading, quit their jobs, or live a luxury lifestyle. The promotion minimizes financial risk and may steer people toward expensive training, misleading investment arrangements, or requests for money and financial information. The polished lifestyle shown in the promotion is part of the sales pitch.
lessons.scammer_says: "I learned this simple trading system and now I make more in a week than I used to make in a month." "Join my training today and learn how to quit your job. The risk is minimal if you follow my system."
lessons.the_trick: The promotion uses social media, success stories, and luxury-lifestyle claims to make quick wealth appear easy. Once interested, the person may be pushed into expensive training or fraudulent investment opportunities and asked for money or financial details.
lessons.consequences: You can lose money on expensive training or a fraudulent investment arrangement. Sharing financial information can create additional risks, and unrealistic expectations can encourage you to take financial risks you would not otherwise take.
danger_signs: The promotion promises quick wealth or suggests you can easily quit your job.
Financial risk is minimized or described as almost nonexistent.
The pitch relies on luxury lifestyles, success stories, or pressure to join.
You are pushed toward expensive training, an investment arrangement, or requests for financial information.
lessons.safe_action: Do not invest or pay for training because of a social-media promise of easy wealth. Research the person and company independently, understand the risks and total costs, and never share banking information simply to qualify for an opportunity.

lessons.title: Tax-Debt Relief Scam
lessons.summary: A company promises to settle your tax debt for pennies on the dollar before checking whether you qualify.
lessons.body: A company advertises that it can settle tax debts for "pennies on the dollar." The pitch may sound like a guaranteed solution, but the company may not first determine whether you actually qualify for meaningful tax relief. Consumers can end up paying large service fees while little or no useful work is done, leaving the underlying tax problem unresolved.
lessons.scammer_says: "We can settle your IRS tax debt for pennies on the dollar." "Pay our enrollment fee today and we'll take care of the IRS for you. Don't worry about whether you qualify — our program is designed to save you thousands."
lessons.the_trick: The company sells the promise of dramatic tax savings before evaluating whether the consumer qualifies. The consumer may pay substantial fees while receiving little useful assistance, while the actual tax debt remains unresolved.
lessons.consequences: You can lose money on service fees while still owing the original tax debt. Delaying attention to the real tax problem can make the situation worse.
danger_signs: The company promises to settle tax debt for "pennies on the dollar" before evaluating your situation.
You are asked to pay substantial fees before knowing whether you qualify.
The salesperson focuses on a dramatic savings promise instead of your actual tax circumstances.
The company does not clearly explain what specific work it will perform for the fee.
lessons.safe_action: Do not pay based only on a promise of huge tax savings. Get the facts about your tax debt directly from the IRS and understand whether you qualify for any relief before paying a company to help. Be especially cautious about large upfront fees and guaranteed-sounding claims.

quizQuestions.question: What is the FIRST thing you should do if someone calls claiming a suspicious bank charge?

options.text: A suspicious charge appeared. I should give my card number to verify.
Hang up and call my bank using the number on my card.
Ask for a supervisor.

quizQuestions.explanation: A key red flag is being asked to share sensitive information or act immediately without verifying through a trusted number.  HANG UP and call back using a known number (from the back of your card, or from your statement).

quizQuestions.question: Why do scammers mention a specific amount like "$2,450"?

options.text: To make the story sound real and get you to share card details.
Your bank always shares exact charge amounts over the phone.
It's proof they work for your bank.

quizQuestions.explanation: If they get your card details, they can buy thousands of dollars in goods online or withdraw cash from ATMs. Your bank account could be emptied in hours, and recovering the money might take months or never happen.  Statements taken from trash cans can give scammers details they use to try to sound legitimate.

quizQuestions.question: What should you NEVER share with a caller claiming to be from your bank?

options.text: Your full name and address.
The 3-digit code on the back of your debit card.
Your last purchase.

quizQuestions.explanation: Hang up immediately. Call your bank using the number on your debit card or their official website (never use the number the caller gives you). Check your account online yourself to see if there's any real problem.

quizQuestions.question: When should you give Medicare ID information over the phone?

options.text: When the Caller ID says Medicare.
When the caller knows my name.
Never.  Medicare will never ask for it.

quizQuestions.explanation: A key red flag is being asked to share sensitive information or act immediately without verifying through a trusted number.

quizQuestions.question: What should you do if you get a Medicare "expiration" call?

options.text: Hang up and call 1-800-MEDICARE yourself.
Press 1 to speak to a representative.
Give your Medicare number to reactivate.

quizQuestions.explanation: With your Medicare and Social Security numbers, they can file fake medical claims, steal your identity for loans, or sell your info on the dark web. This could lead to ruined credit and years of identity theft problems.

quizQuestions.question: True or false: Your Medicare card expires and needs reactivation.

options.text: Your card expires every year.
False — Medicare cards do not expire.
Only if you miss payments.

quizQuestions.explanation: Hang up or ignore the call. Contact Medicare directly at 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227) using a known good number to verify your coverage status. Your Medicare card never expires.

quizQuestions.question: What should you NEVER allow a "tech support" caller to do?

options.text: Send you an email with instructions.
Connect to your computer remotely.
Tell you how to restart safely.

quizQuestions.explanation: A key red flag is being asked to allow a technician to have remote control of your computer.  They can quickly and secretively install software that lets them spy on you, and access accounts like your bank, investments, etc.

quizQuestions.question: A computer pop-up says "Call this number for virus help." What do you do?

options.text: Call the number immediately.
Close the pop-up and ignore it.
Visit their website for the fix.

quizQuestions.explanation: Clicking on those popups can let scammers have remote access that lets them steal passwords, bank info, photos, and personal documents. They can lock your files for ransom or use your computer for illegal activities, making you responsible.  If there is a virus on your computer, take it to a reputable local repair company.

quizQuestions.question: Real tech companies like Microsoft will:

options.text: Never call you directly about computer viruses.
Always charge $199 for repairs.
Need remote access to help.

quizQuestions.explanation: Close the pop-up without calling. Restart your computer in Safe Mode if worried. Run a free scan with antivirus software you trust, like Windows Defender. Never allow remote access to unknown callers.

quizQuestions.question: Someone calls pretending to be your grandchild in jail. What is your first step?

options.text: Send the bail money as requested.
Hang up and call your grandchild's real number.
Ask for their birthdate to verify.

quizQuestions.explanation: Even if they tell you their phone is lost or damaged, it never hurts to call and check. And if they don't answer (they may actually be in school!), call someone you know who would know their whereabouts.

quizQuestions.question: Legitimate emergencies never ask for payment by:

options.text: Personal check.
Wire transfer or gift cards.
Credit card over phone.

quizQuestions.explanation: Wire transfers and gift cards can't be reversed. You lose thousands with no way to recover, and real grandchildren in trouble wouldn't ask for untraceable payments.

quizQuestions.question: A "grandchild in trouble" call asks you to keep it secret because:

options.text: The scammer really doesn't want you to verify the actual location of your grandchild.
Police told them to stay quiet.
It's embarrassing but legitimate.

quizQuestions.explanation: Hang up and call your real grandchild directly using a known phone number. Never send money without verifying in person or through trusted channels.

quizQuestions.question: Utility company threatens disconnection in 30 minutes. What do you do?

options.text: Hang up and call your utility using a phone number on your bill.
Buy the prepaid card they request.
Ask them to email the bill first.

quizQuestions.explanation: Utilities do not call to inform you they are cutting off service.  And a legitimate utility would have no problem if you called back through a trusted number.  (Be sure it's a verified number from your bill, not a number the caller provides.)

quizQuestions.question: Real utility companies accept payment by:

options.text: Bitcoin or prepaid debit cards only.
Check, credit card, or bank account.
Cash at any convenience store.

quizQuestions.explanation: Be suspicious of anyone asking for an unusual payment method.  If you buy prepaid cards and give them the numbers, the money vanishes instantly. No power gets disconnected because it was never your real utility company, and you can't get refunds from these payment methods.

quizQuestions.question: Why won't real utilities disconnect power immediately?

options.text: They send written notice and allow time to pay.
Computer systems take 30 minutes minimum.
Your neighbors would complain.

quizQuestions.explanation: Hang up. Call your utility company using the number on your bill or website. Check your account balance online or in person. Real companies never demand instant prepaid card payments over the phone.

quizQuestions.question: You receive a text about "missed package" that asks for $3.95 payment. What do you do?

options.text: Click link to pay small fee.
Delete it and check real delivery sites.
Call the number to confirm package.

quizQuestions.explanation: Never click a link in a text or email that you were not expecting.  Never call a number in a text or email you were not expecting.

quizQuestions.question: How do real delivery companies charge for any fees due?

options.text: Leave a door tag directing you to pay via the official website, or they send a notice in the mail.
Text unknown numbers for payment.
Call you and demand prepaid gift card numbers over the phone.

quizQuestions.explanation: The fear of missing a package may entice you to click a link. That link may install malware and viruses, or it may take you to a 'phishing' site where it mimics a bank login so they capture your login credentials.

quizQuestions.question: Why do scammers ask for tiny amounts like $3.95?

options.text: Your package is actually cheap.
Small fees seem less suspicious than large ones.
That's standard delivery cost.

quizQuestions.explanation: Delete the text message. Check your real delivery accounts (UPS, FedEx, USPS) using official apps or websites. Real companies leave notices at door.

quizQuestions.question: A disaster charity calls for a credit card donation. What do you do?

options.text: Hang up and donate through known websites.
Give your card information if they promise tax receipt.
Ask for their charity registration first.

quizQuestions.explanation: A key red flag is being asked to share sensitive information or payment information to an unknown caller who pressures you to act immediately without verifying through a trusted number.

quizQuestions.question: What is a safe way to verify charities?

options.text: The Caller ID matches charity name.
Check charitynavigator.org or official site.
They mention recent disaster news.

quizQuestions.explanation: Scammers can use technology to imitate the Caller ID name of a legitimate charity. If you want to donate, hang up and call your charity of choice directly. Never provide donations directly to someone who calls you.

quizQuestions.question: Legitimate charities usually collect donations by:

options.text: Website, mail, or in-person events.
Cold calls asking for credit cards.
Text message links only.

quizQuestions.explanation: Hang up. Donate directly through known charities like Red Cross at redcross.org or local churches. Verify organizations at charitynavigator.org or guidestar.org before giving.

quizQuestions.question: Some calls from the "Refund department". They claim they need to issue a refund and need remote computer access to give it to you. Why?

options.text: To install malware and steal your information.
It's a standard refund processing step.
They can't email the money.

quizQuestions.explanation: The excitement of getting the money distracts from the risk of letting someone install software that could let them control your computer and steal information from it (like bank passwords).

quizQuestions.question: Legitimate refund from stores comes by:

options.text: Direct deposit or check automatically.
Phone call and computer access.
Gift card in the mail.

quizQuestions.explanation: No legitimate refund process requires software installation.

quizQuestions.question: Never download software from:

options.text: People you know.
Unsolicited refund callers.
An official store website.

quizQuestions.explanation: Hang up. Check your real account (Amazon, store website) for legitimate refund notices. Companies deposit refunds automatically or mail checks — never need remote access.

quizQuestions.question: A "mystery shopper" job asks you to send gift card numbers. Is it legitimate?

options.text: You've spotted a scam — hang up immediately.
Try the legitimate first assignment.
Ask for a supervisor to verify.

quizQuestions.explanation: Companies don't offer jobs over the phone without ever talking to you first.  Jobs that ask you to buy something and then be reimbursed are a scam.

quizQuestions.question: Real employers pay by:

options.text: Check, direct deposit, or PayPal.
Gift cards you buy yourself.
Cash at grocery store.

quizQuestions.explanation: You can lose hundreds spent on gift cards. Scammers drain the cards instantly for cash or online purchases. Legitimate employers never ask employees to buy gift cards for payment.

quizQuestions.question: Before accepting mystery shopper job:

options.text: Send gift cards immediately.
Google company name + "scam."
Trust high pay promises.

quizQuestions.explanation: Delete the offer (if it is email) or hang up. Real mystery shopper jobs come from established companies with websites, paychecks, and never require you to buy gift cards. Search company name + "scam" online first.

quizQuestions.question: An online romance asks for an emergency wire transfer. Is this OK?

options.text: Asking for money without ever meeting is a big red flag — it's likely scam.
Real emergencies happen overseas.
Send the money if they promise repayment.

quizQuestions.explanation: If the relationship is emotional but you've never met in real life, do not send money.

quizQuestions.question: Healthy online relationships:

options.text: Never involve sending money.
Include wire transfers for travel.
Start with gift card requests.

quizQuestions.explanation: There have been cases where thousands of dollars were sent over time via wire/gift cards, all unrecoverable. The "sweetheart" disappears after draining resources. Victims lose savings and suffer emotional betrayal.

quizQuestions.question: Romance scammer avoids:

options.text: Text messages.
Live video calls showing face/location.
Social media profiles.

quizQuestions.explanation: Never send money to online contacts. Verify identity through video call or mutual friends. Report to FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (ic3.gov) and dating site. Real relationships develop without money requests.

quizQuestions.question: You receive a call from the IRS about an "unclaimed refund." What do you do?

options.text: Hang up and check irs.gov yourself.
Give my bank routing number so they can make a deposit.
Press 1 to claim immediately.

quizQuestions.explanation: The IRS does not call, they send mail.  Any personal information you give to scammers can be used to commit identity theft, and financial information given to them will be used to access your accounts.

quizQuestions.question: Real IRS refunds arrive by:

options.text: Phone call deposit.
Mail check or existing direct deposit.
Prepaid debit card.

quizQuestions.explanation: Giving scammers bank details let them drain accounts or create fake checks. IRS identity theft leads to tax problems, frozen refunds, and years repairing credit/government records.

quizQuestions.question: The real IRS contacts you by:

options.text: Phone calls asking for bank information.
A letter in the mail.
A text or email message asking you to click a link.

quizQuestions.explanation: Hang up or ignore the text or email. The IRS sends refund checks by mail or direct deposits already on file. Check status at irs.gov using your own computer; never call numbers from unsolicited messages.

quizQuestions.question: Door-to-door roofer asks for a cash deposit now to lock in a discount or schedule. What do you do?

options.text: Say no and get multiple written estimates.
Pay half if the shingles look loose.
